cmimc-2017-algebra-01.title: Set up two equations
cmimc-2017-algebra-01.body:
Let $f$ and $r$ be the original numbers of foxes and rabbits. Then $3f=2r$, so $r=\frac32 f$, and after the moves $10(f-10)=13\cdot\frac r2$.

Substitute: $10f-100=\frac{13}{2}\cdot\frac{3f}{2}=\frac{39f}{4}$, so $40f-400=39f$ and $f=400$, $r=600$.

Left: $(400-10)+\frac{600}{2}=390+300=690$.

**Answer: 690**

cmimc-2017-algebra-01.title: Use a common multiplier
cmimc-2017-algebra-01.body:
Originally foxes : rabbits $=2k:3k$. After the moves: foxes $=2k-10$, rabbits $=\frac{3k}{2}$, and $\frac{2k-10}{3k/2}=\frac{13}{10}$.

So $10(2k-10)=\frac{39k}{2}$, i.e. $40k-200=39k$ giving $k=200$. Foxes left $390$, rabbits left $300$.

**Answer: 690**

cmimc-2017-algebra-02.title: Rewrite in reciprocals
cmimc-2017-algebra-02.body:
Since $x\circ y=\dfrac{1}{\frac1x+\frac1y}$, the operation adds reciprocals. For $x\circ(y\circ z)$:
$$x\circ(y\circ z)=\frac{1}{\frac1x+\frac{1}{y\circ z}}=\frac{1}{\frac1x+\frac1y+\frac1z}.$$
By induction the whole expression equals
$$\frac{1}{\frac12+\frac1{2^2}+\cdots+\frac1{2^{2017}}}=\frac{1}{1-2^{-2017}}=\frac{2^{2017}}{2^{2017}-1}.$$

**Answer: $\dfrac{2^{2017}}{2^{2017}-1}$**

cmimc-2017-algebra-03.title: Compare coefficients
cmimc-2017-algebra-03.body:
Let $P(x)=ax^2+bx+c$. Then $P(P(x))=aP(x)^2+bP(x)+c$, so
$$P(P(x))-P(x)^2=(a-1)P(x)^2+bP(x)+c.$$
If $a\ne1$ this has degree $4$, but the right side has degree $2$, so $a=1$. Then the left side is $bP(x)+c=bx^2+b^2x+(bc+c)$.

Matching: $b=1$, $b^2=1$, $bc+c=2c=2016$, so $c=1008$. Thus $P(x)=x^2+x+1008$ and $P(1)=1010$.

**Answer: 1010**

cmimc-2017-algebra-04.title: Split by parity
cmimc-2017-algebra-04.body:
The $j=3$ term is $\frac{3}{1!}=3$. For $j\ge4$, pair $j=2k$ and $j=2k+1$ ($k\ge2$); both have $\lfloor j/2\rfloor=k$:
$$\sum_{k=2}^\infty\frac{2k+(2k+1)}{k!}=\sum_{k=2}^\infty\frac{4k}{k!}+\sum_{k=2}^\infty\frac1{k!}=\sum_{k=2}^\infty\frac{4}{(k-1)!}+\sum_{k=2}^\infty\frac1{k!}.$$
The first sum is $4(e-1)$ and the second is $e-1-1=e-2$. Total: $4e-4+e-2+3=5e-3$.

**Answer: $5e-3$**

cmimc-2017-algebra-05.title: Periodicity
cmimc-2017-algebra-05.body:
Replacing $x$ by $x+5$ adds $2+3=5$ to the left side and $5$ to $\lfloor x\rfloor$, so $x\in S\iff x+5\in S$.

Checking $[0,5)$ by cases (breakpoints at multiples of $\frac52,\frac53$ and integers) gives exactly
$$[1,\tfrac53),\ [2,\tfrac52),\ [3,\tfrac{10}3),\ [4,5),$$
with lengths $\frac23,\frac12,\frac13,1$, total $\frac52$ per period of length $5$. Every $4$ consecutive intervals form one period, so the first $2016$ intervals have total length $504\cdot\frac52=1260$, and interval $2017$ is the first of a new period, of length $\frac23$.

Sum: $1260+\frac23=\frac{3782}{3}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{3782}{3}$**

cmimc-2017-algebra-06.title: Factor and apply AM-GM
cmimc-2017-algebra-06.body:
Non-real roots come in conjugate pairs, and $P$ has odd degree, so it has a real root of absolute value $1$; it is not $1$ since $P(1)=3$, so it is $-1$. The other four roots are $\alpha,\bar\alpha,\beta,\bar\beta$ with modulus $1$, so
$$P(z)=C(z+1)(z^2-az+1)(z^2-bz+1),\quad a=2\operatorname{Re}\alpha,\ b=2\operatorname{Re}\beta,\ |a|,|b|\le2.$$
$P(0)=C=2$. $P(1)=3$ gives $4(2-a)(2-b)=3$, so with $p=2-a,\ q=2-b\ge0$: $pq=\frac34$.

$P(2)=2\cdot3\,(5-2a)(5-2b)=6(2p+1)(2q+1)=6\,(4pq+2(p+q)+1)=6\,(4+2(p+q))$.

By AM-GM, $p+q\ge2\sqrt{pq}=\sqrt3$, so $P(2)\ge6(4+2\sqrt3)=24+12\sqrt3$, attained at $p=q=\frac{\sqrt3}2$ (i.e. $a=b=2-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$, which satisfies $|a|\le2$).

**Answer: $24+12\sqrt3$**

cmimc-2017-algebra-07.title: Power sums via a recurrence
cmimc-2017-algebra-07.body:
Let $E_r=\sum\frac{a^r}{b+c}$ and $s=a+b+c$. Since $\frac{a^{r+1}}{b+c}+a^r=\frac{a^r\,s}{b+c}$, summing cyclically gives $E_{r+1}+(a^r+b^r+c^r)=sE_r$.

- $r=1$: $32+s=9s$, so $s=4$.
- $r=2$: $122+(a^2+b^2+c^2)=32\cdot4=128$, so $a^2+b^2+c^2=6$, hence $ab+bc+ca=\frac{16-6}{2}=5$.
- $r=0$: $9+3=4\sum\frac1{b+c}$, so $\sum\frac1{4-a}=3$.

Clearing denominators in the last: $\sum(4-b)(4-c)=3\prod(4-a)$, i.e. $48-8s+e_2=3(64-16s+4e_2-e_3)$. With $s=4,e_2=5$: $48-32+5=21=3(64-64+20-e_3)=60-3e_3$, so $e_3=13$.

**Answer: 13**

cmimc-2017-algebra-08.title: Think of 15 numbers in 1..10
cmimc-2017-algebra-08.body:
Equivalently choose $15$ integers $x_i\in[1,10]$ with sum $80$ and consider $\sum x_i^2$. Replacing two values $u\le v$ by $u-1,v+1$ (or the reverse) keeps the sum and changes $\sum x^2$ by $2(v-u)+2$ or $-2(v-u)+2$, so the sum of squares is minimised by making the numbers as equal as possible and maximised by pushing them to the ends $1$ and $10$.

**Minimum:** all values in $\{j,j+1\}$ with $15j+t=80$, $0\le t\le15$ gives $j=5,t=5$: ten $5$s and five $6$s, so $m=10\cdot25+5\cdot36=430$.

**Maximum:** only $1$s and $10$s would need $a_1+10a_{10}=80$, $a_1+a_{10}=15$, giving $a_{10}=\frac{65}{9}$, not an integer, so exactly one value $k\in[2,9]$ must be used once with $14$ numbers in $\{1,10\}$: $a_1+a_{10}=14$, $a_1+10a_{10}=80-k$. Subtracting, $9a_{10}=66-k$, forcing $k\equiv3\pmod9$, i.e. $k=3$, $a_{10}=7$, $a_1=7$. Then $M=7\cdot1+9+7\cdot100=716$.

$M-m=716-430=286$ (confirmed by exhaustive enumeration).

**Answer: 286**

cmimc-2017-algebra-09.title: Count the increments
cmimc-2017-algebra-09.body:
The increment $\lfloor\sqrt{a_n}\rfloor$ takes the value $k$ exactly twice for each $k$ that is not a power of $2$, and three times for each power of $2$ (the perfect squares in the sequence are exactly the powers of $4$; when $a_n=(2^j)^2$ the values $4^j,\ 4^j+2^j,\ 4^j+2^{j+1}$ all have root $2^j$).

So after using increments $1,\ldots,44$ (with powers of two $1,2,4,8,16,32$ counted three times) we have made $2\cdot44+6=94$ steps and reached
$$a_{95}=1+2(1+\cdots+44)+(1+2+4+8+16+32)=1+1980+63=2044>2017.$$
The previous term is $a_{94}=2044-44=2000<2017$, so $N=95$ (also confirmed by direct computation).

**Answer: 95**

cmimc-2017-algebra-10.title: Roots must stay bounded
cmimc-2017-algebra-10.body:
If $\alpha$ is a root of $P$, putting $z=\alpha\pm c$ shows $(\alpha+c)^2$ and $(\alpha-c)^2$ are roots too. By the parallelogram law $|z-c|^2+|z+c|^2=2(|z|^2+c^2)$, so one of $|z\pm c|^2$ is at least $|z|^2+c^2$. Choosing that one each time, $|z_{k+1}|\ge|z_k|^2+c^2$, and $|z|^2+c^2>|z|$ always holds when $c>\frac12$ (since $(|z|-\frac12)^2+c^2>\frac14$). That gives infinitely many distinct roots, impossible. So $c\le\frac12$.

For $c=\frac12$: equality forces roots with $|z-c|=|z+c|$ (purely imaginary) and $|z|=\frac12$, so the only possible roots are $\pm\frac i2$, with equal multiplicity. Indeed $P(z)=z^2+\frac14$ works: $\left((z-\frac12)^2+\frac14\right)\left((z+\frac12)^2+\frac14\right)=(z^2-z+\frac12)(z^2+z+\frac12)=(z^2+\frac12)^2-z^2=z^4+\frac14$.

Hence $P(z)=(z^2+\frac14)^n$, $n\ge1$ (leading coefficient must be $1$). Then $P(\frac13)=\left(\frac{13}{36}\right)^n$ and
$$\sum_{n\ge1}\left(\tfrac{13}{36}\right)^n=\frac{13/36}{23/36}=\frac{13}{23}.$$

**Answer: $\dfrac{13}{23}$**
